conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to hear, in your own words, how things have been going for you emotionally over the past seven days. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; there’s no judgment—just support. I’ll ask ten gentle questions, one at a time. When you’re ready, we can start.

1. In the past week, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly… not much. I used to laugh at little things my husband said or at silly videos, but lately it feels like I have to force it. Even when something is funny, the smile fades pretty fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… I might chuckle once or twice, but it feels kind of hollow, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I’ll make plans—like meeting a friend for coffee or taking the baby for a walk—but when the time comes, it feels like a chore. I still go, but that excited feeling I used to get just isn’t there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not feeding him well enough or I missed his sleepy cues. I know rationally it’s not all on me, but the guilt just pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, but my chest feels tight and my mind races—what if he stops breathing? What if I’m not watching closely enough? I check on him again and again even when nothing’s wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, a few times this week. It hits out of nowhere—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even though everything looks normal. It passes after a bit, but it’s scary while it lasts.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, I haven’t showered, and it feels like I’m drowning. I’ll sit on the couch staring at it all, wondering how I’ll ever catch up, even when I know the list isn’t that long.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been my nights lately. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—playing the day over, worrying I messed something up, imagining scary “what-ifs.” Sometimes I drop off, then I’m wide awake again at two or three and can’t settle for an hour or more.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there. I’ll be feeding the baby or folding laundry and feel tears coming for no clear reason. It’s not every second, but it’s definitely more “sad” than “okay.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
A few times this week. Once it was just because the baby wouldn’t nap—nothing huge—but I sat in the rocker with tears streaming down. It feels so silly afterward, but in the moment I can’t stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t felt that way. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter comes rarely and feels hollow, plans you once looked forward to now feel like chores, and most days carry a gray cloud of sadness or spontaneous tears. You described tight-chested worry that arrives even when your baby is safe, sudden panicky surges, and nights spent wide awake with racing thoughts. Everyday tasks feel overwhelming and you often blame yourself when things go wrong, even though part of you knows that isn't fair. Despite feeling exhausted, you have not had thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, hollow laughter, clearly diminished enjoyment—closest to "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports clear loss of anticipatory pleasure—plans feel like chores and lack excitement—aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses frequent, automatic self-blame despite rational awareness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, excessive worry about infant safety despite no danger, aligning with 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage basic tasks, and emotionally paralyzed—matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly trouble falling and staying asleep due to racing thoughts and worry, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness on most days, spontaneous tears, and a persistent "gray cloud" mood matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 22 falls well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major depression in the postpartum period. The pattern of <sym>depressed mood most days</sym>, marked <sym>anhedonia</sym>, disproportionate <sym>guilt</sym>, prominent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym>, plus sleep disruption unrelated to infant needs, aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Functional impairment is evident in her description of routine tasks feeling drowning. No self-harm ideation reduces immediate safety risk but does not lessen clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss results and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and, if needed, <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these screening responses with your clinician so they can complete a full diagnostic evaluation
4. Enlist practical help overnight-partner, family, or postpartum doula-to allow at least one 4-5 hour stretch of sleep; practice wind-down routine of 20 min quiet activity when awakened by worry
5. Reach out today to a support group or helpline for new mothers; talking reduces isolation and provides coping ideas
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress once treatment starts
7. If you ever do have thoughts of self-harm, treat it as an emergency-call 911, go to your nearest emergency department, or call a suicide prevention line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: _____________  
Clinician: _____________  

Presenting complaints (patient report)  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days  
- Marked loss of enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities  
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety/racing thoughts; episodic panic sensations  
- Disproportionate self-blame and guilt regarding infant care  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks  
- Initial and middle insomnia related to ruminative worry  
- No self-harm ideation endorsed  

Observed pattern  
Responses cluster around:  
1. Core depressive symptoms (sad mood, anhedonia, guilt, crying)  
2. Prominent anxiety symptoms (free-floating worry, panic attacks)  
3. Functional impairment (household tasks “drowning,” sleep disruption)  

Screening significance  
- Elevated concern for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features  
- No current safety risk (denied self-harm)  

Next steps (per protocol)  
- Score responses on Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (document numeric score)  
- Provide education on postpartum mood/anxiety disorders  
- Offer referral for expedited clinical assessment and evidence-based intervention  
- Arrange follow-up within 1 week to review status and support plan
